caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 405 of 1978, With C.R. No. 1169 (s) of 1979
lawyer:
B. N. Chowdhury ----- For the appellant
A. Khaleque ----- For the respondent.
parties:
Amulla Kumar Ghose  ----- Appellant
Vs.
Khama Prava Haldar ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
I have heard Mr. B. N: Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the appeal and Mr. Md. Abdul Khaleque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent. Perused the judgment and examined the evidence on record Mr. B. N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the appeal, has urged that the Court of appeal below erred in not considering that in view of the defendant denial of having received any quit notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, the burden would be however upon the plaintiff to prove the existence of any such notice and said burden could never be discharged without examining the postal peon as to service and this having not been done in the instant case the Court of appeal below erred in holding that notice was duly issued and tendered. He has next urged that the Court of appeal below came to a Ending of fact erroneously without considering the witnesses for the defendant and the surrounding circumstances of the case as to the question of the defendant being a defaulter Mr. A. Khaleque, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent, on the other hand, has urged that in view of provisions of section 114 (1) of the Evidence Act there would exist a legal presumption in the facts of the instant case to the effect that the notice had reached the addressee in due course after it had been proved to have been posted and the legal presumption being in favour of the plaintiff the burden would be upon the defendants to prove otherwise. He has further urged that Court of appeal below on a consideration of the evidence on record and particularly the fact that in the absence of any complaint made by the defendant as to looting of his articles of the grocer shop on his return from India with any police station and on a consideration of the evidence of the defendant himself to the effect that he never did know as to who had looted his articles but only heard about it from others who never came to depose, came to a finding that there existed no looting and hence no salish and also no award as to which salish there is also no documentary evidence and hence it could not be said that the Court of appeal below came to a finding of fact as to the defendant being a defaulter upon a non-consideration of the material witnesses for the defendants. There is enough substance in the contentions of the learned Advocate and it needs to be sustained. The only point that arises for the disposal of the appeal is whether the defendant was legally found to be defaulter and whether a notice under section 106 of the T.P. Act was validly issued and tendered. On a reference to the evidence on record it is seen that the notice under section 106 of the T.P. Act was posted at the office address of the defendant as to which address no exception was taken by the defendant at the time of hearing of this appeal or at the trial. It is further seen that the postal cover under which the notice was sent bears the endorsement of the postal peon to the effect that it was refused. Now, the defendant argues that the same would not by itself be an evidence of due service unless it would be corroborated by the postal peon and prove the endorsement and its refusal. There is no substance in this contention also because if a letter is found to have been properly addressed and posted but returned with the endorsement. "refused", the presumption under section 114(f) of the Evidence Act would be that it was presented to the addressee and he had refused to receive it and in such a case it would not be necessary to call the postal peon to prove the endorsement and refusal. This is well settled and supported by a number of decisions and of good authorities. In the case reported in 27 C.W.N. at page 1073, a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court in deciding a similar matter as to notice terminating a tenancy observed in the relevant portion thus:- 

 6. I am in respectful agreement with the observations above which are in complete accord with the view I have taken hereinbefore to the effect that when a letter is properly addressed and posted but was returned with the endorsement "refused" the presumption would be that it was presented to the addressee and that he refused to receive it and the proof of the endorsement would be enough to prove a valid service and it would not be necessary to call the postal peon to prove the endorsement and the refusal. In that view of the matter I find no substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant to the effect that the postal peon ought to have been examined to prove the endorsement and refusal in order to constitute a valid service.
